title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: the son keeps saying 'teach me more.' why doesn't the father sigh?

segments.voice: Yesterday in tat tvam asi, the honey: juices of many trees made one, and the tiger still a tiger. Shvetaketu asked for more again. Today, the rivers.

Sunday dinner at a friend's house. Different food, a different grace before the meal, and somehow the same jokes about a cousin who's always late. It raises one question: where do all these different people come from? Uddalaka answers with water. One river runs east. Another runs west. They never meet on any map. But both end in the sea.
screen: `SUNDAY DINNER, ANOTHER TABLE.` → `WHERE DO WE ALL COME FROM?` → `EAST, WEST, ONE SEA.`

segments.voice: These rivers, my dear, the father says, the eastern ones flow east and the western ones flow west. From the sea they go to the sea. They become the sea itself, and there they don't know, I am this river, I am that one. In the same way, he says, all these creatures, having come out of Being, don't know that they have come out of Being. Whatever they are here, tiger or lion or gnat, that they become. The differences stay. What's missing is only the knowing. Then the refrain: that is the self; that you are. A neighbor tradition has its own line about where people come from. In the Christian Bible, in the book of Acts, the apostle Paul, speaking in Athens, says God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Here's what they share. People who look and live very differently come from one source, and are more alike than they know. And the honest difference. Paul speaks of God who made the nations: a maker, and the made. Uddalaka speaks of Being as the very self of each one, the river already made of sea. Two old answers to one question, each in its own words.
screen: `FROM THE SEA, TO THE SEA.` · `NO RIVER SAYS: I AM THIS ONE.` · `OF ONE BLOOD ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `MAKER AND MADE, OR ONE SELF.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let each breath come in like a river and go out like one. Don't sort them, this breath, that breath; just let them arrive and leave. Rest on the father's words: from the sea they go to the sea.
Tat tvam asi: that you are. The rivers come from the sea, go back to the sea, and never knew they'd left it.
Your line: tat tvam asi, from the sea, to the sea, east and west alike. Until next time.

howItsDone: In Vedanta study, the rivers of Chandogya 6.10 are read right after the honey of 6.9. Acts 17:26 is part of the Christian New Testament, from Paul's speech in Athens.

fork.setup: two cousins who grew up on opposite coasts meet and argue about whose side of the family is the 'real' one. what does the river picture point out?

fork.reveal: eastern and western rivers both come from the sea and go back to it. creatures come from Being and don't know it; the father points at the knowing.

original.note: Sanskrit: the sea. In the Chandogya, rivers go from the sea to the sea and become the sea itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: unity means everybody turns out to be the same.
what it means: rivers keep their courses, yet all come from the sea and go back to it; only the knowing is missing.
what a scholar hears: 6.10.1, from the sea to the sea (samudrat samudram), read beside Acts 17:26 without making them one teaching.

chat.says: Sam's grandma said 'of one blood all nations' at dinner. it's from Acts. same as tat tvam asi?
options: close, not the same: both see one source for all people; in Acts, God made them.
exactly the same teaching, just said at a church dinner table instead.
nothing alike: a Bible verse and an Upanishad can't share anything.
chat.meaning: Acts 17:26 and the rivers both see all peoples coming from one source. Paul speaks of God who made the nations; Uddalaka, of Being as each one's self.

Uddalaka.meaning: the father teaching his son in the Chandogya

Acts.meaning: a New Testament book about the early church

Paul.meaning: an apostle whose travels and speeches fill much of Acts

tat tvam asi.meaning: that you are: the refrain after each picture

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.10.1–3 (the eastern rivers flow east, the western west; from the sea they go to the sea and become the sea itself, and there do not know 'I am this one, I am that one'; so all creatures, having come from Being, do not know they have come from Being; whatever they are here, tiger, lion, wolf ... that they become; that which is the finest essence ... that you are, Shvetaketu; please, sir, teach me more)

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): Acts 17:26 quoted from the KJV; please verify wording. Setting: Paul's speech in Athens (Acts 17:22 onward). Shared: people who look and live differently come from one source. Honest difference: Paul speaks of God who made the nations (maker and made); Uddalaka of Being as the very self of each one. No ranking, no 'all the same'. A Christian reviewer should confirm the framing and the howItsDone line. 'Are more alike than they know' is the lesson's summary of what the two share, not a claim either text makes in those words.
Priya storyline (1751–1764, day 6): Sunday dinner at Sam's; his grandmother (churchgoing, as in day 1679) says Acts 17:26 at the table. This is the month's best-friend family touchpoint.

Practice kind: eyes-closed stillness. Surprising fact: the rivers come FROM the sea as well as return to it.
